title: The first foot pedal and Emil Gonzalez the drum repairman
summary: Hazel describes the earliest bass drum foot pedal in detail and recommends Emil Gonzalez, a drum mechanic and collector who might still have one.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Early drum kits and the gear drummers used

blocks.x: Mark, do you remember the first foot pedal for the bass drum that you ever saw? Yeah. About when?

I can't remember when, the date, but I can describe it to you. It had a long metal rod. And on the end of the rod was the beater. And then there was a, in the end of the beater, there was a little screw thing that was sort of a, triangle in shape. And you fit a leather strap through that. And you fit a leather strap through that. And you fit a stuff the foot part of it was wood, well that hooked into like a, oh like these, anything that you, like the mailman's straps, you know, a deal like that, and then it hooked into the pedal, and the pedal was, had a metal housing, you might call it, and then to get the leverage, the spring was on the top of the bass drum, and it fit into a hole in this long rod, in one end of the spring, and the other end, it had like a fork, that would fit on the shell, the rim of the bass drum, like that, to keep it steady, you see, and you could, they had a, a tension knot on there, where you could loosen it, or tighten it to your individual taste, and that's, that's, that, I think, I'm not positive, but I think that was the first foot pedal ever made, I mean that's, that's, that's the way, that's the first one I ever saw, Which head did it hit? That's the way it was, huh? Which head did it hit? Which head of the drum did it hit? The inside, the inside, the inside, did it hit from above? It hit in the, exactly in the middle, but the, the leverage was from above, yeah, the spring, you see, the spring was, was, and when, when, if you hit it, well then, when you let it go, it would, but the spring, didn't, well it was not built into the pedal, it was on the top of the bass drum, and, and, and, fit into a hole, and, in this, this long, uh, rod, and that the ball, was on the end of that rod, and then the bottom of the ball, like I tell you, had this little thing where you fit the strap into, and the strap in turn fit into the, into the wooden pedal, the wooden pedal, and that, the wooden pedal, was held by, a, steel frame, or iron frame, whatever it was, that's the earliest pedal that I can recall, there may be a couple of them around here, yeah, some of the real old timers, should, should, should have one of them, Did you have, no, I don't think he, they might pick one up, you know, I'll tell you, there's only, there's only, there's only about one fellow that I know of, around here, who might have one, Bill, there's a fellow by the name of Emil Gonzalez,

I don't know, but he would, because he, he used to fix all of our heads, tuck our heads, and, and fix all of our drums for, for us, you know, he, he, he was the man. How was the action, did you ever play around, did it sing fast, or, oh, well, you, like I tell you, they had a, they had a, what's called them that you could regulate it, the way you, But it was, very, it was very shaky, Bill, you see?

No, it wasn't, it, it, it wasn't compact, and naturally, so it was shaky, and it was the only way that they could, in those days, the only way they could build, But you couldn't, you couldn't, when you, when you'd hit down like that, it would, it, this, the bottom part of it, they would shake like that, and it wasn't reliable, like the, later pedals became.
Where's Emil Gonzalez's family? Are they around, you know?

They did live on Gainia Street somewhere, out around, none say, around Constance Street, between Constance and Chapitulis. At Gainia? It's about the, about the 1200, about the 11 or 1200 block, coming up from Canal Street, and he may have one, because he had everything, he was a guy like Tom Brown, that collected everything, you know, and he had everything that you could ever imagine, that pertained to drums, and he, incidentally, was a very good mechanic, he could do more with it, and he, of course, in those days, everything was wood, too, no metal drums.
